doc.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Grandparents' victrola and the 1920s records
summary: Raised on Long Island, he wound his grandparents' victrola and fell for the energy of 1920s records and old TV shows over 1950s pop.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well I’m curious as to what — in your childhood or teen years or something — turned you on to the music from the twenties and thirties?

I actually started when I was like five years old. I was born in Brooklyn and raised out in Smithtown, Long Island. And my grandparents remained in Brooklyn and every holiday we would come and do holiday things — whether it was Mother’s Day, Thanksgiving, birthdays, Christmas, all that stuff. And they used to have a lot of parties in the twenties and thirties, family gatherings, where people brought old records, old phonograph records. They were married in 1922. And one day my grandmother points to this old victrola and shows me how to wind it up, and there was this array — there was like two thousand old records, everything from Grand Opera to novelty singers of the time, of the twenties, to an actual Louis Armstrong Okeh and a King Oliver Brunswick. So I would just be enthralled about winding up the machine and actually help produce this music by putting it on. And growing up in those years there was these wonderful hits like “How Much is that Doggie in the Window” and “Oh My Papa.” And Lord, even as a kid, I said this is really corny stuff, it really is. And what I was hearing on these old discs was this great energy and this great vitality that I did not hear at the popular music of my time, the mid-fifties. And also coming home after school everyday you could still turn on your T.V. and see Laurel & Hardy, you could see the “Our Gang,” “The Little Rascals” and the old black and white cartoons, which had elements of 1920s and early 30s jazz in it. This was still part of it. And those were my reinforcements. Like wow, there’s my music so to speak. And I know I was this weird kid. Because everyone else was keeping up in the times and I would just be constantly drawn to searching out what I could find out about this music. And even watching T.V. shows like Joe Franklin, who was a fellow here in New York who is still around, and Max Morath. These would also be people who said yes this is old stuff but it’s classic stuff, it’s great stuff.
And it was pop music at the time, right? Or not?
Uh the pop music that I was listening to from the twenties, yeah it was pop and jazz.
But your grandparents would have listened to that as popular music.
Oh yes sure. Yeah. Well jazz in the 1920s was popular music. It was the Jazz Age so to speak and not everyone really knew what jazz was and called it a lot of different things. It
was probably — the twenties and thirties was really so great that the majority of the people would appreciate this new music.
